extracted.intended_audience: law professors, patent attorneys, judges, and law students interested in patent claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for interpreting patent claims (sources of meaning, role of text vs policy, appellate review, extrinsic evidence, and administrative alternatives). Focused on doctrinal debate between textualist and anti-textualist approaches to claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim language is the best evidence of what ideas it is trying to convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article emphasizes that claim language should be treated as primary evidence of meaning; to say one must know the idea before understanding language is a conceptual error. (See text: "claim language is the best evidence of what ideas it is trying to convey.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction should consider multiple documentary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction routinely considers the claim structure, the specification, the prosecution history, dictionaries, and expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markman and subsequent cases direct courts to consult these sources in construing claim terms; the Article lists these five categories explicitly as the traditional sources for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as the best source for technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The best source for understanding a technical term is the specification from which it arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (e.g., Multiform Desiccants) favor the specification over other sources when a term is technical or originated in the patent document itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dictionaries in claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some precedents favor consulting dictionaries to determine ordinary meaning of claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tex. Digital Sys. v. Telegenix is noted as favoring dictionaries; Phillips en banc questioned whether primary reliance should be on dictionaries or on patentee's use in the specification. The Article also cites criticisms of over-reliance on dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history is a core evidence source for construing claim meaning and boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts commonly consult prosecution history along with the specification and claims; it is listed among the documentary sources considered in claim construction cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of expert testimony and extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony and other extrinsic evidence can be used to explicate claim terms, particularly technical ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commentators (e.g., Nard) favor expert testimony; there is disagreement about the extent to which trial courts should receive and rely on such evidence versus treating construction as purely legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent indeterminacy of claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claim language may be inherently indeterminate; the nature of language makes it impossible to capture the full essence of an invention solely in claim text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (Burk & Lemley, Lee, Liivak) argue that claim text often cannot yield a single determinate boundary; this supports the view that courts inevitably must shape boundaries when words are underdetermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textualism vs anti-textualism (methodological approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competing interpretive philosophies: textualism (focus on claim text/plain meaning) versus anti-textualism (focus on the patentee's invention, functional scope, or policy outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article discusses these camps at length, noting labels like 'hypertextualism' (claim-centered) and 'pragmatic textualism' or invention-centered approaches; it emphasizes that the debate underlies claim-construction disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Phillips yields no clear answer, policy may inform construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive and policy considerations should come into play only when traditional claim construction does not yield a clear answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed by commentators like Lee and some others: reserve non-textual/policy factors for gap-filling after ordinary interpretive tools are exhausted to avoid 'redrafting' claims while still addressing underdeterminate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents as narrow exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents allows a court to deem an unclaimed product to be infringing if the difference is 'insubstantial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine is described as a narrow exception to the rule that claims define the bounds of the monopoly; cases like Warner-Jenkinson and commentary about its waning application are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the invention / claims as measure of the grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims afford the measure of the grant to the patentee and define the invention's boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational cases (e.g., Merrill, Milcor Steel) and treatises emphasize that it is the claims that determine what the patent excludes others from doing; this principle underpins textualist approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate standard of review for claim construction (de novo v. deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim construction is reviewed de novo on appeal or given deference to trial-court factual findings is contested: Cybor held de novo review, while others argue for deference to trial courts on factual predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article recounts Cybor's en banc holding for de novo review and opposing views that favor deference (e.g., calls for 'something approaching' deference for factual predicates or clear-error review for fact findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial court's role in evaluating extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial courts are positioned to gauge the relevance and need for additional evidence to explicate claim terms, including taking evidence at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eastman Kodak v. Goodyear is cited for the proposition that trial judges are best situated to assess the need for extrinsic evidence, in tension with Cybor's legal-question approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative alternatives and PTO involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts could (or should) refer claim-interpretation questions to the Patent Office (PTO), and the PTO could make dictionary selection and related decisions more predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (e.g., Duffy; Miller & Hilsenteger) argue administrative routes—allowing the PTO to play a role—could increase predictability and consistency in claim meaning and dictionary choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: broader claim language increases invalidity risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad claim language may favor patentees by covering more, but it also increases the likelihood that the claim will be invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes the practical tradeoff: broader claims can be powerful if valid, but their breadth raises vulnerability to invalidity challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: considering dictionaries before the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism exists of practices that place dictionary definitions ahead of the specification when construing claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Hattenbach and others criticize 'process of considering dictionaries before specifications' as problematic; Phillips en banc asked parties to address whether dictionaries or patentee's usage in spec should be primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where indeterminacy exists, courts must shape the boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: When linguistic or textual indeterminacy is present, courts will be required to shape the appropriate boundary of the patent grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burk & Lemley and others emphasize that indeterminacy is inevitable and that courts are inevitably called upon to make normative choices to set boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction may decide the case
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide what the claims legally mean is often functionally to decide the patent case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities such as Wang Labs. and Markman (and quoted commentary) observe that claim-meaning determinations frequently determine infringement and validity outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention-centered (pragmatic) vs claim-centered framing of patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators favor construing claims narrowly 'in light of the actual invention' (invention-centered) rather than relying solely on the claim text (claim-centered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burk & Lemley, Liivak, Nard, and others are discussed: invention-centered approaches conceptualize the invention functionally, potentially permitting courts to construe claims to reflect the actual invention rather than isolated words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability outside litigation matters for interpretive regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictability of claim meaning outside litigation (for practitioners and the public) is an important goal of an interpretive regime and may weigh in evaluating methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lefstin and others argue that regimes should prioritize predictability outside of litigation as a metric of success for claim-construction doctrine.
